claim: The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology (RPCB) was established to provide evidence about reproducibility in basic and preclinical cancer research.
source: The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology (RPCB) was established to provide evidence about reproducibility in basic and preclinical cancer research, and to identify the factors that influence reproducibility more generally.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as the purpose of the RPCB project.

claim: The RPCB was established to identify the factors that influence reproducibility more generally.
source: The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology (RPCB) was established to provide evidence about reproducibility in basic and preclinical cancer research, and to identify the factors that influence reproducibility more generally.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as one of the goals of the RPCB.

claim: Research in psychology, economics and the social sciences is usually conducted on humans with the goal to identify causal relationships that generalize to other humans.
source: First, research in psychology, economics and the social sciences is usually conducted on humans and the goal is to identify causal relationships that generalize to other humans.
evidence: This is stated as a contrast to cancer biology research, drawing on established knowledge about these fields.

claim: Research in cancer biology is conducted in tissue cultures and non-human animals with the goal to identify causal relationships that generalize to living humans.
source: In contrast, research in cancer biology is conducted in tissue cultures and non-human animals, and the goal is to identify causal relationships that generalize to living humans.
evidence: This is stated as a contrast to psychology and social sciences research, based on established knowledge of cancer biology research practices.

claim: Claims about causal relationships made by cancer biologists are always dependent on a more extensive set of assumptions about the relationship between experimental systems and real-world settings.
source: This means that the claims about causal relationships made by cancer biologists are always dependent on a more extensive set of assumptions – which are fallible – about the relationship between experimental systems and real-world settings.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the difference between animal/tissue culture models and human disease.

claim: As many as 19 of 20 cancer drugs put into clinical development never demonstrate enough safety, efficacy or commercial promise to achieve licensure.
source: In clinical testing, as many as 19 of 20 cancer drugs put into clinical development never demonstrate enough safety, efficacy or commercial promise to achieve licensure (Hay et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hay et al., 2014.

claim: Cancer drugs that achieve licensure often show underwhelming efficacy in trials.
source: Even those few that run the gauntlet from trialing to license often show underwhelming efficacy in trials (Davis et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davis et al., 2017.

claim: Poorly planned, executed and reported research efforts can divert attention and resources from more productive endeavors.
source: The initial response of many researchers to the COVID-19 pandemic clearly showed how poorly planned, executed and reported research efforts can divert attention and resources from more productive endeavors (London and Kimmelman, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to London and Kimmelman, 2020, referencing COVID-19 pandemic research.

claim: Many translation failures reflect the intrinsic challenges of conducting research at the cutting edge of what we understand about disease.
source: As one of us (JK) and Alex London have argued, many of these failures reflect the intrinsic challenges of conducting research at the cutting edge of what we understand about disease (London and Kimmelman, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to London and Kimmelman, 2015.

claim: The failure of numerous drugs inspired by the amyloid cascade hypothesis in part reflects uncertainties about the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease.
source: The failure of numerous drugs inspired by the amyloid cascade hypothesis, for example, in part reflects uncertainties about the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease.
evidence: This is presented as an example of how theoretical uncertainties lead to translation failures.

claim: Properly designed and analyzed trials provide important feedback on experimental models and pathophysiological theories when translation failures are due to theoretical uncertainties.
source: When translation failures are due to theoretical uncertainties like this, properly designed and analyzed trials provide important feedback on experimental models and pathophysiological theories (Kimmelman, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimmelman, 2010.

claim: Only 17 out of the 50 originally planned Replication Studies in the RPCB were completed.
source: As mentioned previously, only 17 out of the 50 originally planned Replication Studies were completed, with varying degrees of success: five reproduced important parts of the original research articles; six produced equivocal results; two could not be interpreted; and four did not reproduce the experiments they attempted to reproduce (an additional six replication reports were only partially completed).
evidence: This is a direct report of the RPCB results.

claim: Five RPCB replication studies reproduced important parts of the original research articles.
source: As mentioned previously, only 17 out of the 50 originally planned Replication Studies were completed, with varying degrees of success: five reproduced important parts of the original research articles; six produced equivocal results; two could not be interpreted; and four did not reproduce the experiments they attempted to reproduce (an additional six replication reports were only partially completed).
evidence: This is a direct report of the RPCB results.

claim: Six RPCB replication studies produced equivocal results.
source: As mentioned previously, only 17 out of the 50 originally planned Replication Studies were completed, with varying degrees of success: five reproduced important parts of the original research articles; six produced equivocal results; two could not be interpreted; and four did not reproduce the experiments they attempted to reproduce (an additional six replication reports were only partially completed).
evidence: This is a direct report of the RPCB results.

claim: Two RPCB replication studies could not be interpreted.
source: As mentioned previously, only 17 out of the 50 originally planned Replication Studies were completed, with varying degrees of success: five reproduced important parts of the original research articles; six produced equivocal results; two could not be interpreted; and four did not reproduce the experiments they attempted to reproduce (an additional six replication reports were only partially completed).
evidence: This is a direct report of the RPCB results.

claim: Four RPCB replication studies did not reproduce the experiments they attempted to reproduce.
source: As mentioned previously, only 17 out of the 50 originally planned Replication Studies were completed, with varying degrees of success: five reproduced important parts of the original research articles; six produced equivocal results; two could not be interpreted; and four did not reproduce the experiments they attempted to reproduce (an additional six replication reports were only partially completed).
evidence: This is a direct report of the RPCB results.

claim: The initial estimate of the Positive Predictive Value of the diagnostic machine is 47%.
source: For simplicity we assume that 50% of the equivocal results would regress on repetition, leading the diagnostic machine to recommend advancing with three of these studies. Adding these three studies to the five studies that reproduced important parts of the original research articles, and dividing by 17 replication attempts, gives us an initial estimate of 47% for the Positive Predictive Value of the diagnostic machine.
evidence: This is calculated from the RPCB data with an assumption about equivocal results.

claim: Replication rates for articles in three leading journals in psychology were 40%.
source: To put this number in context, replication rates for articles in three leading journals in psychology were (depending on how you count) 40% (Open Science Collaboration, 2015); the figure for articles in two leading journals in economics was 66% (Camerer et al., 2016); and for articles in the social sciences published in Nature and Science the figure was 67% (Camerer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Open Science Collaboration, 2015.

claim: Replication rates for articles in two leading journals in economics was 66%.
source: To put this number in context, replication rates for articles in three leading journals in psychology were (depending on how you count) 40% (Open Science Collaboration, 2015); the figure for articles in two leading journals in economics was 66% (Camerer et al., 2016); and for articles in the social sciences published in Nature and Science the figure was 67% (Camerer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Camerer et al., 2016.

claim: Replication rates for articles in the social sciences published in Nature and Science was 67%.
source: To put this number in context, replication rates for articles in three leading journals in psychology were (depending on how you count) 40% (Open Science Collaboration, 2015); the figure for articles in two leading journals in economics was 66% (Camerer et al., 2016); and for articles in the social sciences published in Nature and Science the figure was 67% (Camerer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Camerer et al., 2018.

claim: 33 RPCB studies were abandoned due to cost overruns, difficulties in securing research materials, or a lack of cooperation from the original authors.
source: As mentioned previously, according to the Editors' summaries, 2 of the 17 published Replication Studies reported findings that could not be interpreted (due to unexpected challenges in repeating the original experiments), and 33 studies were abandoned due to cost overruns, difficulties in securing research materials, or a lack of cooperation from the original authors.
evidence: This is a direct report of the RPCB results.

claim: 26% of original authors were extremely helpful in the RPCB.
source: The RPCB team found that the original authors were bimodal in their helpfulness when it came to providing feedback and sharing data and materials: 26% were extremely helpful, but 32% were not at all helpful or did not respond (Errington et al., 2021c).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Errington et al., 2021c.

claim: 32% of original authors were not at all helpful or did not respond in the RPCB.
source: The RPCB team found that the original authors were bimodal in their helpfulness when it came to providing feedback and sharing data and materials: 26% were extremely helpful, but 32% were not at all helpful or did not respond (Errington et al., 2021c).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Errington et al., 2021c.

claim: The RPCB team did not observe a relationship between material sharing and replication rates.
source: Laboratories that were more confident about the reproducibility of their original publications, or more fastidious with their record keeping, might be more likely to cooperate with the RPCB than laboratories that were more doubtful or less fastidious (although the RPCB team did not observe a relationship between material sharing and replication rates; Errington et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Errington et al., 2021b.

claim: The lower bound estimate of the Positive Predictive Value is 16% based on intention to treat analysis.
source: Based on what has been reported thus far by the RPCB, eight replication studies produced results consistent with original research articles. The remaining 42 replication studies did not, thus providing a lower bound on the Positive Predictive Value of 16% – an estimate that is not far off from the proportion of studies Amgen reported reproducing years ago (Begley and Ellis, 2012).
evidence: This is calculated from the RPCB data using an intention to treat approach, with reference to Begley and Ellis, 2012.

claim: The RPCB meta-analysis covered a total of 158 different effects.
source: As mentioned previously, the meta-analysis covered a total of 158 different effects.
evidence: This is a direct report of the RPCB meta-analysis scope.

claim: Most of the original effects in the RPCB meta-analysis were positive effects (136).
source: Most of the original effects were positive effects (136), and for these the RPCB team found that the median effect size in the replications was 85% smaller than the median effect size in the original experiments; moreover, in 92% of cases the effect size in the replication was smaller than in the original.
evidence: This is a direct report of the RPCB meta-analysis results.

claim: For positive effects in the RPCB, the median effect size in the replications was 85% smaller than the median effect size in the original experiments.
source: Most of the original effects were positive effects (136), and for these the RPCB team found that the median effect size in the replications was 85% smaller than the median effect size in the original experiments; moreover, in 92% of cases the effect size in the replication was smaller than in the original.
evidence: This is a direct report of the RPCB meta-analysis results.

claim: In 92% of cases in the RPCB, the effect size in the replication was smaller than in the original.
source: Most of the original effects were positive effects (136), and for these the RPCB team found that the median effect size in the replications was 85% smaller than the median effect size in the original experiments; moreover, in 92% of cases the effect size in the replication was smaller than in the original.
evidence: This is a direct report of the RPCB meta-analysis results.

claim: The abstracts of 13 of the 17 Replication Studies (76%) noted at least one experimental claim that did not reproduce the original effect.
source: According to our estimates, the abstracts of 13 of the 17 Replication Studies (that is, 76% of the studies) noted at least one experimental claim that did not reproduce the original effect (meaning that, had replication studies been submitted as original publications, their 'stories' would have been less coherent, putting them at higher risk of rejection by a journal).
evidence: This is based on the authors' analysis of the RPCB replication study abstracts.

claim: Only 58% of animal studies are eventually published.
source: To our knowledge there have been no attempts to assess the NPV of a field of research, possibly because many negative outputs are never written up, never mind submitted to a journal; indeed, according to one estimate, only 58% of animal studies are eventually published (Wieschowski et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wieschowski et al., 2019.

claim: Preclinical researchers are unable to predict whether replication studies will reproduce experiments.
source: On the one hand, forecast studies carried out by one of us (JK) and colleagues have found that: (i) preclinical researchers are unable to predict whether replication studies will reproduce experiments (Benjamin et al., 2017); (ii) cancer experts perform worse than chance in predicting which treatments tested in randomized trials will show efficacy (Benjamin et al., 2021); (iii) the predictions of cancer experts about trial outcomes are also heavily influenced by the format in which evidence is presented to them (Yu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Benjamin et al., 2017.

claim: Cancer experts perform worse than chance in predicting which treatments tested in randomized trials will show efficacy.
source: On the one hand, forecast studies carried out by one of us (JK) and colleagues have found that: (i) preclinical researchers are unable to predict whether replication studies will reproduce experiments (Benjamin et al., 2017); (ii) cancer experts perform worse than chance in predicting which treatments tested in randomized trials will show efficacy (Benjamin et al., 2021); (iii) the predictions of cancer experts about trial outcomes are also heavily influenced by the format in which evidence is presented to them (Yu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Benjamin et al., 2021.

claim: The predictions of cancer experts about trial outcomes are heavily influenced by the format in which evidence is presented to them.
source: On the one hand, forecast studies carried out by one of us (JK) and colleagues have found that: (i) preclinical researchers are unable to predict whether replication studies will reproduce experiments (Benjamin et al., 2017); (ii) cancer experts perform worse than chance in predicting which treatments tested in randomized trials will show efficacy (Benjamin et al., 2021); (iii) the predictions of cancer experts about trial outcomes are also heavily influenced by the format in which evidence is presented to them (Yu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2021.

claim: Expert communities are able to pick out which studies replicate in psychology.
source: For example, some studies suggest that expert communities are – in the aggregate – able to pick out which studies replicate in psychology (Dreber et al., 2015) and the social sciences (Camerer et al., 2018), and experts appropriately update their beliefs about an experimental phenomenon on seeing new and more powerful evidence (Ernst et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dreber et al., 2015.

claim: Expert communities are able to pick out which studies replicate in the social sciences.
source: For example, some studies suggest that expert communities are – in the aggregate – able to pick out which studies replicate in psychology (Dreber et al., 2015) and the social sciences (Camerer et al., 2018), and experts appropriately update their beliefs about an experimental phenomenon on seeing new and more powerful evidence (Ernst et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Camerer et al., 2018.

claim: Experts appropriately update their beliefs about an experimental phenomenon on seeing new and more powerful evidence.
source: For example, some studies suggest that expert communities are – in the aggregate – able to pick out which studies replicate in psychology (Dreber et al., 2015) and the social sciences (Camerer et al., 2018), and experts appropriately update their beliefs about an experimental phenomenon on seeing new and more powerful evidence (Ernst et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ernst et al., 2018.

claim: Assuming a base rate of 10%, NPV of 99%, and PPV of 47%, the sensitivity of the diagnostic machine is 92% and the specificity is 88%.
source: If we assume that the PPV is the higher of the two estimates we derived earlier, 47%, then the sensitivity of the diagnostic machine is 92% and the specificity is 88% (see Box 2 for the relevant formulae).
evidence: This is calculated from the assumed parameters using diagnostic test formulas.

claim: A PPV of 47% translates to a likelihood ratio for all positive preclinical studies of 8.
source: This translates to a likelihood ratio for all positive preclinical studies of 8: that is, the diagnostic machine is eight times more likely to recommend clinical testing for real causal effects than for null effects.
evidence: This is calculated from the diagnostic test parameters.

claim: Using the lower PPV estimate of 16%, the positive likelihood ratio drops to 1.7.
source: However, if we use the 'intention to treat' principle and adopt the lower estimate of the two estimates for PPV, 16%, the positive likelihood ratio drops to 1.7, driven by a sharp fall in the specificity.
evidence: This is calculated from the lower PPV estimate using diagnostic test formulas.

claim: The 17 published RPCB studies are likely biased in favor of work that is reproducible.
source: It might be tempting to view the 33 abandoned efforts as uninformative, but we may be able to actually learn from them because it is likely that the 17 published studies are biased in favor of work that is reproducible.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of study completion and abandonment.

claim: Laboratories that were more confident about the reproducibility of their original publications might be more likely to cooperate with the RPCB.
source: Laboratories that were more confident about the reproducibility of their original publications, or more fastidious with their record keeping, might be more likely to cooperate with the RPCB than laboratories that were more doubtful or less fastidious (although the RPCB team did not observe a relationship between material sharing and replication rates; Errington et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is speculation about potential selection bias in the RPCB.

claim: The RPCB selected experiments that did not rely on unusual samples or techniques, which probably increased the chances of successful replication.
source: The RPCB also selected experiments that did not rely on unusual samples or techniques, which probably increased the chances of successful replication: experiments that require unusual samples or techniques are, it seems to us, more likely to require more attempts to get them 'to work', and therefore more likely to be prone to the problem of 'researcher degrees of freedom' (Simmons et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference about the RPCB selection criteria and its effect on replication success, with reference to Simmons et al., 2011.

claim: The RPCB team experienced problems with important information not being included in the original research articles.
source: The problems the RPCB team experienced in terms of important information not being included in the original research articles, or the original authors not sharing data and/or reagents (Errington et al., 2021c), also points to a diagnostic machine whose workings are often opaque and that leaves a very patchy audit trail for its outputs.
evidence: This is reported based on the RPCB team's experience, with citation to Errington et al., 2021c.

claim: The RPCB team experienced problems with original authors not sharing data and/or reagents.
source: The problems the RPCB team experienced in terms of important information not being included in the original research articles, or the original authors not sharing data and/or reagents (Errington et al., 2021c), also points to a diagnostic machine whose workings are often opaque and that leaves a very patchy audit trail for its outputs.
evidence: This is reported based on the RPCB team's experience, with citation to Errington et al., 2021c.

claim: If the original publications represented unbiased estimates of real effects, one would expect the replications to regress towards smaller effect sizes as often as they drifted towards larger effect sizes.
source: If the original publications represented unbiased estimates of real effects, one would expect the replications to regress towards smaller effect sizes as often as they drifted towards larger effect sizes.
evidence: This is based on statistical principles about regression to the mean.

claim: Similar regression has been seen in other large-scale replication projects.
source: Similar regression has been seen in other large-scale replication projects and noted by other commentators (Colquhoun, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Colquhoun, 2014.

claim: The RPCB only tried to reproduce papers asserting positive causal relationships.
source: Unfortunately the RPCB (and similar projects) only tried to reproduce papers asserting positive causal relationships, thus providing no information about how often the diagnostic machine falsely labels submissions as 'negative'.
evidence: This is a description of the RPCB methodology.

claim: The 158 effects analyzed in the RPCB included 22 null effects.
source: (Although the 158 effects analyzed included 22 null effects, these were embedded in papers that contained mostly positive results, so they are unlikely to be representative of the broader population of negative results.)
evidence: This is a direct report of the RPCB meta-analysis composition.

claim: To the authors' knowledge, there have been no attempts to assess the NPV of a field of research.
source: To our knowledge there have been no attempts to assess the NPV of a field of research, possibly because many negative outputs are never written up, never mind submitted to a journal; indeed, according to one estimate, only 58% of animal studies are eventually published (Wieschowski et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: All the papers selected for the RPCB had received high numbers of citations.
source: All the papers selected for the project had received high numbers of citations, meaning that they had made an impact among cancer researchers: moreover, many of them had been published in high-profile journals such as Cell, Nature and Science, although this was not one of the selection criteria.
evidence: This describes the RPCB sampling approach.

claim: Many of the papers selected for the RPCB had been published in high-profile journals such as Cell, Nature and Science.
source: All the papers selected for the project had received high numbers of citations, meaning that they had made an impact among cancer researchers: moreover, many of them had been published in high-profile journals such as Cell, Nature and Science, although this was not one of the selection criteria.

claim: Publication in high-profile journals was not one of the RPCB selection criteria.
source: All the papers selected for the project had received high numbers of citations, meaning that they had made an impact among cancer researchers: moreover, many of them had been published in high-profile journals such as Cell, Nature and Science, although this was not one of the selection criteria.
evidence: This clarifies the RPCB methodology.

claim: The principal diagnostic property directly assessed by the RPCB was the Positive Predictive Value.
source: Therefore, the principal diagnostic property directly assessed by the project was the Positive Predictive Value, which is defined as the number of outputs that replicated (true positives) divided by the total number of outputs tested.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what the RPCB methodology measures.

claim: Assuming a base rate of 30% and PPV of 47%, the positive likelihood ratio drops to 2.
source: For example, if we were to assume the base rate of true hypotheses is 30% and the PPV is 47%, then the positive likelihood ratio drops to 2, which constitutes extremely weak evidence.
evidence: This is calculated from the assumed parameters.

claim: A positive likelihood ratio between 1 and 2 is considered weak evidence.
source: Typically, a positive likelihood ratio between 1 and 2 is considered weak evidence, while ratios between 2 and 10 constitute moderate evidence, and ratios higher than 10 constitute strong evidence.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1 caption.

claim: Positive likelihood ratios between 2 and 10 constitute moderate evidence.
source: Typically, a positive likelihood ratio between 1 and 2 is considered weak evidence, while ratios between 2 and 10 constitute moderate evidence, and ratios higher than 10 constitute strong evidence.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1 caption.

claim: Positive likelihood ratios higher than 10 constitute strong evidence.
source: Typically, a positive likelihood ratio between 1 and 2 is considered weak evidence, while ratios between 2 and 10 constitute moderate evidence, and ratios higher than 10 constitute strong evidence.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1 caption.

claim: With the most generous set of numbers, preclinical studies of the type sampled in the RPCB provide only moderate evidence that a clinical hypothesis is true.
source: Even with the most generous set of numbers, preclinical studies of the type sampled in the RPCB (that is, studies that receive high numbers of citations) provide only moderate evidence that a clinical hypothesis is true.
evidence: This is an inference based on the likelihood ratio calculations.

claim: The positive likelihood ratio increases with the PPV for a given value of the base rate.
source: The positive likelihood ratio (y-axis) increases with the PPV (x-axis) for a given value of the base rate (see color code).

claim: For a given value of the PPV, the positive likelihood ratio decreases as the base rate increases.
source: However, for a given value of the PPV, the positive likelihood ratio decreases as the base rate increases.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1.

claim: The basic and preclinical research enterprise can be likened to a vast 'diagnostic machine' that determines which clinical hypotheses should be advanced for further development.
source: We liken the basic and preclinical cancer research enterprise to a vast 'diagnostic machine' that is used to determine which clinical hypotheses should be advanced for further development, including clinical trials.
evidence: This is the central analogy proposed by the authors.

claim: The results of the RPCB suggest that the diagnostic machine currently recommends advancing many findings that are not reproducible.
source: The results of the RPCB suggest that this diagnostic machine currently recommends advancing many findings that are not reproducible.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RPCB results.

claim: False positives occur when research communities mistakenly conclude that a clinically promising causal relationship exists when it does not.
source: False positives occur when research communities mistakenly conclude that a clinically promising causal relationship exists when it does not.
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors.

claim: False negatives occur when a real and potentially impactful causal relationship is assumed to be too weak to be clinically promising, or the relationship is not observed in the first place.
source: False negatives occur when a real and potentially impactful causal relationship is assumed to be too weak to be clinically promising, or the relationship is not observed in the first place.
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors.

claim: The cost to society of missing out on impactful cancer treatments can be considerable.
source: However, in the context of preclinical cancer research, false negatives require serious consideration because the cost to society of missing out on impactful cancer treatments can be considerable, especially given that clinical development exists to cull false positives but can do little about false negatives.
evidence: This is a value judgment about the importance of false negatives.

claim: Clinical development exists to cull false positives but can do little about false negatives.
source: However, in the context of preclinical cancer research, false negatives require serious consideration because the cost to society of missing out on impactful cancer treatments can be considerable, especially given that clinical development exists to cull false positives but can do little about false negatives.
evidence: This is an inference about the function of clinical development in the research pipeline.

claim: Unforced errors in drug development are a sort of tax or friction that makes the research process significantly less efficient than it could be.
source: These unforced errors are a sort of tax or friction that makes the research process significantly less efficient than it could be.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the impact of reproducibility failures.

claim: Many of the issues that lead to unforced errors – haste, poor study design, biased reporting – are relatively easy and cheap to fix.
source: Many of the issues that lead to such errors – haste, poor study design, biased reporting – are relatively easy and cheap to fix.
evidence: This is a judgment about the tractability of addressing reproducibility issues.

claim: Given the prevalence of preclinical studies that do not reproduce according to Amgen and Bayer, the gains of reducing unforced errors could be substantial.
source: And given the prevalence of preclinical studies that do not reproduce according to Amgen and Bayer, the gains of reducing such unforced errors could be substantial.

source: If a treatment is advanced to clinical research based on such an error, medicine is deprived of an opportunity to develop an effective treatment and, furthermore, the research enterprise is deprived of the opportunity to learn something about the generalizability of our models and theories.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of false positives.

claim: If a treatment is advanced to clinical research based on an unforced error, the research enterprise is deprived of the opportunity to learn something about the generalizability of models and theories.

claim: Replacing devotion to a p-value of 0.05 with a more demanding value such as 0.005 would require researchers to use much larger sample sizes in their experiments.
source: Moreover, some of the costs associated with redesigning the diagnostic machine so that it produces fewer false positives are likely to be significant: for example, replacing our religious devotion to a p-value of 0.05 with an even more demanding value, such as 0.005 (Benjamin et al., 2018), would require researchers to use much larger sample sizes in their experiments.
evidence: This is based on statistical principles, with reference to Benjamin et al., 2018.

claim: Larger sample sizes would mean testing fewer clinical hypotheses, limiting the ability to scan the vast landscape of plausible hypotheses.
source: In medicine, however, the total volume of human talent, tissue samples and non-human animals available to researchers is limited, so larger sample sizes would mean testing fewer clinical hypotheses, thus limiting our ability to scan the vast landscape of plausible hypotheses.

claim: False negatives might take longer to correct because scientists have less motivation to repeat negative experiments.

claim: False negatives will be especially costly in underfunded research areas like neglected diseases and pediatric cancers.
source: False negatives will be especially costly in underfunded research areas like neglected diseases and pediatric cancers, since errors will not be quickly corrected by competing labs conducting research in parallel.
evidence: This is an inference about the differential impact of false negatives across research areas.

claim: Future studies of reproducibility in the clinical translation process will need to use qualitative research and methods from decision science to characterize how decisions are made about starting clinical development.
source: Future studies of reproducibility in the clinical translation process will need to use qualitative research and methods from decision science to characterize how decisions are made about starting clinical development, what experts believe about the prospects of successful translation, what sorts of evidence they rely on to form these beliefs, and how these beliefs are aggregated to arrive at the institutional decision of the sponsor.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: Preclinical studies should never be interpreted in isolation from other theory and evidence.
source: First and most obviously, preclinical studies should never be interpreted in isolation from other theory and evidence.
